models.best: Inferred from its principle that favours create lasting obligations, kin and neighbours can give ongoing visits, childcare and practical help to someone in distress, so care rests on trust rather than fees. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gifts create a duty to return them, people who can repay with favours and standing may receive more care, while people with no kin, or whose illness stops them giving back, may be left without help and stigma may attach to them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances the work it can do against household needs, relatives can shift their labour to care for a member at home, so the person stays in familiar surroundings. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves the household, care is carried unpaid by whoever is at home, and a household short of labour may have no one free to care for a sick member, so people without relatives may get little support. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects tribute or taxes and redistributes stored goods, a common fund can pay for shared psychiatric and psychological care for people in need, whatever their household means. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates stored goods to officials and central institutions first, local patients may wait longer or receive less, and the care given can depend on the favour of those who hold the stores. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output depends on the labour of enslaved people, owners have a financial reason to treat illness that stops work, so some basic care may be given, but only as a cost of production. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that enslaved people are denied property and rights, their mental health care depends on the owner's decision alone, illness is treated as a loss of labour, and the enslaved have no route of appeal against neglect or punishment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord who gives protection and justice in return for labour can keep a sick tenant on the manor, so the person stays among people who know them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are owed for land and protection, a tenant who can no longer work may lose the land and the protection tied to it, and care depends on the lord's judgement rather than on any professional standard. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guild statutes set training, supervision and quality, practitioners of care could learn under licensed masters and work to standards set in statute. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that guilds limit entry and set prices, the number of licensed practitioners may be kept low, so waiting times stay long and fees stay high, and newcomers without a master may be shut out. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a trade surplus depends on a productive population, the state can pay for care that keeps workers healthy and at work, since illness that cuts output is a national loss. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production for national ends, care may be judged by its effect on output, so people judged unable to work may get little care and may be placed in state institutions rather than treated in their own communities. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land funds the state, care could be paid for from the land tax, leaving wages and grain trade untaxed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, care for people in towns and in non-farm work may be treated as an unproductive cost, so services for urban patients may be funded last. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets and private contracts reward good providers, patients can choose among private therapists and clinics, and competition may lower prices and widen supply. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state stays out except to protect property and contracts, people who cannot pay for therapy or psychiatric treatment may have no public provision, waiting times and stigma are left to the market, and the sick may fall into poverty. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, the choices of patients and providers can show where care is needed without a planner who must guess. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that no planner can gather the knowledge needed, state plans and cheap credit can build clinics and places in the wrong locations and at the wrong scale, so later patients face waiting lists when the capacity proves unsuitable. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a smaller state and fewer controls on markets let private providers and insurers compete, patients may gain choice of therapists and clinics, and competition may add capacity. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that fewer controls leave insurers and providers to set their own terms, mental health cover may be narrower than cover for physical illness, waits may lengthen where private providers find care unprofitable, and costs may fall on the patients least able to pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public spending rises in slumps, mental health services can be expanded when unemployment and distress rise, so that care is available when people are most likely to need it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The federal mental health parity law of 2008 and its evaluations shows how a coverage rule can change little. An analysis of Medical Expenditure Panel Survey data for 2005 to 2013 found no statistically significant change in use of mental health care, how much was used, or total and out-of-pocket spending. The authors judged the effects slight, left open whether plans were already compliant, and more recent evaluations may exist. A model that steers care through rules and budgets carries this risk if it does not measure use and costs. Source: Psychiatric Services (2019), Medical Expenditure Panel Survey analysis; ASPE, TruvenHealth report on the impact of parity (February 2019)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive providers work inside a legal order that curbs monopoly, social insurance can pool the risk of mental illness while many providers compete for patients. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly and organises social insurance, rules set around large insurers and established providers may shut out new and small providers, and people whose illness keeps them out of work may fall outside insurance cover. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft

models.best: Inferred from its principle that universal public services are paid for by high taxes, psychological and psychiatric care can be free at the point of use for everyone, and active labour-market policy can help people with mental illness return to work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that national budgets pay for universal services, care can be rationed by the budget when taxes are under strain, and services run from the centre may leave local needs and stigma unaddressed, so waiting lists can grow when spending is held down. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries and disciplines firms by performance, the same tools could steer public funds to care providers that meet clear targets for waiting times and recovery. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks priority industries, mental health care may receive less credit and fewer resources than favoured sectors, and performance targets may reward high throughput over quality, so short appointments and early discharge may be rewarded. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the rent of land should fund public services, a tax on land values could pay for community psychiatric and psychological services, so the cost falls on land rent rather than on wages. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land values rise where people cluster, a land tax would raise most in prosperous areas, so care funded from land rent may be uneven, with poorer districts and rural areas receiving less for mental health care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example replace wage competition, a small community can provide care for its members through shared work and daily contact, without charge to the member. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities built by example depend on members' goodwill, care may depend on the energy of a few leaders, may lapse when a community fails, and people outside the community may be left with no provision at all. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Trieste and the closure of Italy's asylums shows worker cooperatives, with round-the-clock community services and supervised housing, taking the place of an asylum, which fits this model's aim that workers keep the value of their work. The sources give no hard outcome measures, and some are commemorative or essayistic.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts depend on members' own contributions, people with no income or no place in a mutual group may be left without care, and small mutual funds may be too thin to cover long treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Trieste and the closure of Italy's asylums shows worker cooperatives taking the place of an asylum: Trieste announced in January 1977 that it would close its asylum, full closure came in 1980, and round-the-clock community services, supervised housing and worker cooperatives took its place. The sources give no hard outcome measures, such as readmission rates, and some are commemorative or essayistic.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members control the firm and share its surplus, care may be shaped for the members who run it, staff and insiders may gain more than patients who are not members, and outsiders may have little say in what is provided. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that care is shared according to need within federated communes, people who are ill can receive support from the commune as a matter of course, with no wages or contracts to negotiate. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no contract, nothing guarantees a right to care, and a commune that judges a person to be a burden or a danger may exclude them with no outside body to appeal to. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations run industry directly, the staff who deliver care can run services themselves, so those who give care also decide how it is given. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes are the main lever, care can be disrupted by industrial action, and union leaders may press staff terms above patients' needs, leaving people without treatment during disputes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT

models.best: Inferred from its principle that municipal and national public enterprise, pursued by democratic and gradual means, can build a national minimum of care that every resident can use. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Gradual reform through municipal and national action can stop short of its aims. Trieste and the closure of Italy's asylums shows this: Trieste announced in January 1977 that it would close its asylum, full closure came in 1980, and Italy's statute of May 1978 began the phase-out, yet implementation varied so widely that in some places institutions were only renamed. The sources give no hard outcome measures, such as readmission rates, and some are commemorative or essayistic. Source: Centre for Medical Humanities, review of The Man Who Closed the Asylums (secondary); American Journal of Psychiatry, obituary of Franco Basaglia, 1924 to 1980

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control through guild-like councils, the staff who give care and the people who use it could decide together how services run, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers set the terms of work, staff interests may outweigh patients' needs in decisions about hours, caseloads and admissions, and the state, as one partner among several, may lack the power to correct the balance. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set investment and staff, the state can direct beds and clinicians to where they are needed and provide care free of charge in large numbers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Soviet psychiatry and the diagnosis of sluggish schizophrenia shows how a diagnosis can be turned against dissent. In the Soviet Union it was applied to political dissenters, and clinicians kept using it until 1989. Under this model the state owns the main enterprises and plans investment, so the same authority may be used against critics. Most of the material is secondary, and the results give no case-level detail on Bukovsky or Gorbanevskaya. Source: Stanford, 2019 paper on sluggish schizophrenia as a diagnosis for political dissenters; geohistory.today essay on Snezhnevsky and Soviet political abuse of psychiatry (secondary)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices under public ownership, care services can be run to a budget and a price signal, with a central board setting the rules and the investment. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that managers follow prices, care that is priced may be rationed by what patients can pay, managers may cut services that do not cover their costs, and the central board may give mental health care low investment priority. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that distribution follows need once classes disappear, care would be given according to need rather than ability to pay. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case of Soviet psychiatry and the diagnosis of sluggish schizophrenia shows a diagnosis applied to political dissenters, and clinicians kept using it until 1989. Under this model care follows need, and until the state withers away it is the state that judges need, so whoever judges need may use that power against critics. Most of the material is secondary, and the results give no case-level detail on Bukovsky or Gorbanevskaya. Source: Stanford, 2019 paper on sluggish schizophrenia as a diagnosis for political dissenters; geohistory.today essay on Snezhnevsky and Soviet political abuse of psychiatry (secondary)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that key sectors stay in public hands while markets and special economic zones grow, public hospitals can keep core psychiatric services under public control while private clinics compete for other demand. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that price reform proceeds gradually under party direction, fees for care may rise before public provision reaches poorer areas, and priorities for mental health care may be set by the party rather than by patients' needs. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, patients and staff can shape the services they use, and caring jobs are balanced in complexity so that no one is left with only the hardest work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan through repeated rounds of proposals, urgent care may wait for several rounds before a service can act on a clear need, so waiting times may lengthen. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, workplace health and training can be planned and funded across whole industries, and the state can direct resources to services quickly. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that industry is directed toward national goals, including war, care may be ranked by its use to those goals, and people judged unfit for national work may be denied treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law

models.best: Inferred from its principle that zakat redistributes wealth to people in need, care for those who cannot pay can be funded from zakat, and profit-and-loss finance shares the risk of clinics and training between providers and their funders. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited, credit for building clinics, buying equipment and training staff may be harder to obtain, shared-risk finance may leave small providers without capital, and charity may leave gaps where zakat falls short of need. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, small local care services can be personal and unhurried, matched to the patient's life, and free of coercion where possible. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production stays small and local, specialist staff, equipment and beds for severe illness may be too few to serve every area, so people with serious conditions may have to travel far or wait for treatment elsewhere. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property and small enterprise keep decisions close to people, and subsidiarity leaves care with the smallest competent body, so services stay close to the patient. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that subsidiarity leaves decisions with the smallest competent body, care may depend on what small local bodies can afford, and areas with weak local resources may get little, with no central guarantee to fill the gap. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a social floor guarantees everyone a basic level of provision, mental health care can be treated as part of that floor rather than cut to meet growth targets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that growth is not required and public budgets stay within planetary limits, care must compete for a fixed share with other social needs, and waiting lists may become the way care is rationed among people in need. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, people with mental illness could seek care without losing their income or proving need, and money worries may ease. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that income is paid unconditionally, the income itself does not pay for therapists, clinics or psychiatric beds, so if services are left to the market, people may still face long waits and high fees even with money in hand. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government that issues its own currency can fund care and staff without a fixed cash limit, so capacity can grow when demand rises, with inflation rather than debt as the limit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, shortages of trained staff and beds may go unrecognised as limits, so spending could outrun the clinicians and places that can be supplied, pushing up prices and waiting times without adding care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities who share a resource design, monitor and enforce their own rules, local networks of patients, families and staff could run shared care services and check their quality themselves. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that local communities set and enforce their own rules, local norms may exclude people with mental illness or stigmatise them, and the wider institutions meant to protect them may act slowly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: Public funding for psychological and psychiatric care as a universal right, delivered through round-the-clock community services and worker cooperatives under one set of standards. Budgets are held steady across the economic cycle, and every diagnosis and detention is reviewed by an independent body.
compromise.details: Keeps: community services and worker cooperatives from Trieste and the closure of Italy's asylums (Cooperative economy, Mutualism); public funding that rises in slumps (Keynesian welfare capitalism). Blocks: diagnosis used against critics, as in Soviet psychiatry and the diagnosis of sluggish schizophrenia (Command socialism), safeguarded by independent review of every diagnosis and detention; rationing by ability to pay (Classical laissez-faire capitalism), safeguarded by a free core service (Nordic social democracy); budget cuts in booms (Keynesian welfare capitalism), safeguarded by a fixed budget floor; local exclusion and stigma (Commons governance), safeguarded by a national right to care. Test: waiting times, readmission rates, out-of-pocket spending and stigma, against matched areas over at least five years, with plan compliance checked, since the Trieste sources give no hard outcome measures, the Soviet material is mostly secondary and parity evaluations left compliance open. Source: Centre for Medical Humanities; Stanford, 2019; Psychiatric Services, 2019; Keynes, The General Theory; Smith, The Wealth of Nations; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism; Ostrom, Governing the Commons.
